name: Agouti-related peptide
lead: Agouti-related peptide (AgRP) is a hypothalamic neuropeptide that raises appetite and lowers energy use by blocking melanocortin signalling. It is the natural counterpart to the melanocortin peptides (such as alpha-MSH) that suppress hunger, and it is relevant to physique goals because it is one of the brain's main hunger switches, central to how body fat is regulated [1][2].

AgRP is made in neurons of the hypothalamic arcuate nucleus, which co-release neuropeptide Y; these neurons are switched on by fasting and by ghrelin and are restrained by leptin and insulin [3][4][5]. AgRP was identified in 1997 as an antagonist of the melanocortin 3 and 4 receptors [6][18].

Research on AgRP is laboratory and clinical-physiology work rather than a consumer product. A registered phase 2 trial listed a safety study of AgRP inhibition for obesity and weight loss (n=100) [7], and other registered studies examine AgRP levels alongside growth hormone treatment [8]. Because it is an endogenous signal, people in appearance communities mostly discuss it in terms of hunger control and leanness.

chain: AgRP neurons drive hunger when energy is low
Blocking melanocortin receptors reduces satiety signalling
Hunger and energy expenditure set body-fat level
angle.text: AgRP is the brain's hunger signal; understanding it explains why appetite rises during dieting and why drugs targeting the melanocortin pathway are studied for weight control. It is a biological target rather than something people take.

paras: AgRP neurons increase food intake and reduce energy expenditure when the body is in negative energy balance [2][5]. Experiments in mice show that rapid activation of these neurons is sufficient to start feeding, and that they are needed for feeding in adults [9][10]. AgRP blocks MC3R and MC4R, the receptors through which POMC-derived peptides signal fullness [6][1].

Ghrelin, the stomach hunger hormone, acts on these neurons [11]. Leptin acting on inhibitory neurons dampens their tone toward POMC neurons [12]. AgRP neurons also help control other processes, including liver autophagy during energy deprivation [13] and reproductive hormone axes in obesity [14].
Reviews describe AgRP/NPY and POMC neurons as potential obesity treatment targets [5]. A small pilot study examined how prolonged exercise affects circulating AgRP [15].

Registered trials include a phase 2 safety study of AgRP inhibition for obesity (NCT00779519) [7], growth hormone and liraglutide effects on AgRP in healthy adults [8], and AgRP in preeclampsia [16]. No consumer AgRP product is described in the literature.

timeline.event: AgRP characterised as an antagonist of central melanocortin receptors [6].
Co-expression of Agrp and NPY in fasting-activated neurons reported [17].
AgRP/NPY neurons shown to be essential for feeding in adult mice [10].
Rapid activation of AgRP neurons shown to drive feeding [9].

card.summary: The brain's own hunger-driving peptide that blocks satiety receptors; studied as a lever for appetite and body-fat control.

quick.overview:
AgRP is a peptide made by hunger-sensing neurons in the hypothalamus. When energy runs low, these neurons fire and push appetite up while lowering energy use.

It matters for people working on leanness because it is one of the pathways that makes dieting feel hard, and researchers study it as a target for weight control.
quick.mechanism: AgRP blocks melanocortin 3 and 4 receptors, cancelling the fullness signal from POMC neurons. The same neurons release NPY and GABA for fast hunger drive.
quick.risks: AgRP is an endogenous signal rather than a drug, and no approved therapy targets it directly. Changing this pathway affects appetite, metabolism and growth/reproductive axes.
